You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The failing test `testPValueNearZero` creates a dataset with increasing dimension and asserts that the p-value returned by PearsonsCorrelation.getCorrelationPValues() remains greater than zero, specifically testing a very small p-value (~1E-303). The bug report indicates that the precision of the p-value calculation is limited by machine epsilon, causing very small p-values to drop to zero.

Inspecting the code of `getCorrelationPValues()`, we see that it computes a t-statistic from the correlation coefficient, then uses a T-distribution cumulative probability to calculate the p-value as 2 * (1 - cumulativeProbability(t)).

Looking into the T-distribution's `cumulativeProbability(double)` method, it translates the t-value into an evaluation of the regularized Beta function, which is used to compute the CDF of the t-distribution.

The `regularizedBeta` function delegates to an overloaded version with higher precision parameters (`epsilon` and `maxIterations`). Inside this, when x is less than some threshold, it evaluates a continued fraction to compute the regularized incomplete beta function using logarithms and exponentiations to manage numerical underflow/overflow.

The logBeta function computes the logarithm of the beta function using gamma functions.

From the chain of method calls and the bug report, the issue is that for very extreme t-values leading to extremely small p-values, the numerical precision of `regularizedBeta` and thus the CDF of the t-distribution is limited by the defaults and ultimately machine epsilon. Because of this limitation, p-values are reported as zero instead of diminishing smoothly to very small values beyond about 2.2e-16.

Hence, the failure relates to insufficient numerical precision in `TDistributionImpl.cumulativeProbability`, specifically in its use of `Beta.regularizedBeta` and the underlying continued fraction approximation where machine epsilon limits achievable precision, resulting in the p-value dropping directly to zero for small values rather than a continuous decrease.

This explains why the test which expects to see a small positive p-value around 1e-303 fails, matching the symptoms described in the bug report referencing a similar issue (MATH-201) about machine epsilon limiting precision.

Overall, the bug arises because the probability calculation method (through regularizedBeta) cannot handle the very small probabilities reliably due to floating point precision limits and the numerical algorithms used.

Next, it would be ideal to check if there are any parameters controlling epsilon in the Beta function call or T-distribution that could be modified to improve precision, or if the numerical algorithms in regularizedBeta could be improved to handle extreme tails better. 

After the diagnosis is confirmed, the best classes and methods to fix are likely:

- `org.apache.commons.math.distribution.TDistributionImpl.cumulativeProbability(double)`
- `org.apache.commons.math.special.Beta.regularizedBeta(double, double, double, double, int)`

These represent the level at which numerical precision affects the computed p-values in the correlation statistics.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
